utterances.text: I was born on the 13th of November, 1949.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: I was born in the village of Kruskovo Polje, in the municipality of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Where do you live now?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: Now I live in Bosanski Samac, in the settlement of Brace Jugovica BB.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us something about your educational background? Where did you complete your primary school, secondary school, and all the other schools that you may have completed?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: Some of the years of the primary school I completed at the village of Kruskovo Polje, and the other part I completed in Bosanski Samac. The secondary school, I also completed in Bosanski Samac. And further education I followed in Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us: What's your occupation, and what is that further education, this tertiary education that you then followed?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: That is the higher technical school, and I'm a mechanical engineer by occupation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Are you employed?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us where?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: Currently I'm working at the Ministry of Defence, Samac department.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Sir, did you serve in the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: No, I did not serve in the Yugoslav People's Army. The thing is, is that I was following the medical check-up regarding my ability to serve in the Yugoslav People's Army in 1966. I was declared unfit to serve, for medical reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I would just ask you a few more questions in relation to your political membership. Were you a member of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: For the first time, I was employed in 1973, at the secretariat of the interior, and it was impossible to work for this institution without being a member of the League of Communists. So after I was employed at that institution, I became a member of the League of Communists, and I was a member of the League of Communists until its break-up.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: After that, were you a member of any other political party, and are you now a member of a political party?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: From then I was not a member of any political party, and I am not a member of any political party now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Just a couple of more questions in relation to your personal information. Are you married?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you have children?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. I have a son and a daughter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us: What's your ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: I'm a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: You already said that from 1973 you have been employed at the public security station in Bosanski Samac. Now a few questions in relation to this. Can we clarify something: First of all, what was your job at the police station in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: I was an inspector for fire prevention.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: At that time, from 1973 onwards, was Mr. Zaric at any time chief of the public security station?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: At that time, it was called the secretariat of the interior, and Mr. Zaric was, for a time, the secretary of the secretariat of the interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: This work that you did, that is, the preventing fires, what is the department of the police station, of the public security station? To which department did it belong?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: As part of the secretariat of the interior, there were several organisational units, and one of them was the crime department, which had its own branch office in Doboj. As part of that crime department, there were also the tasks of the inspector for fire prevention.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, your job and your work that you carried out, that was part of the crime department. Is that correct? Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And you said already - I just wanted to clarify - you were subordinated to the centre in Doboj; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And Mr. Zaric, as the secretary at the time, was he your superior?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: He was not my superior, because the work that I did was independent, and all the decisions that I took were in relation to fire prevention, and I was the one who signed these decisions and documents. So I had independence in my work, but I belonged to that organisational unit, that is, the crime department, according to the internal organisation of the employment posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: What were your relations with Mr. Zaric?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: Correct, and we kept a certain distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So you were not friends with Mr. Zaric, you did not go to each other's houses, you did not socialise? That was not the case, then?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: No. He was a functionary. I was an employee. And we did not go to each other's houses. We did not socialise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Until when did you work at the public security station in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: I worked there until the 31st of December, 1987.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And where did you get a job after that?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: After that, I moved to the secretariat for National Defence, actually, to the reporting centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: We will go back to the reporting centre and explain a little bit the functions of that centre. But before that, I would like to ask you a few more questions about certain things that could be of interest. Did you ever carry a weapon?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: No, I did not. I didn't -- I never possessed a weapon. I never possessed a weapon privately.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I would like to briefly now go to another topic. Sir, were you a member of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: No, I was not, because I wasn't a military conscript, so I wasn't a member of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the 4th Detachment, about the fact that it existed in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. I heard that the 4th Detachment was formed, in the media, over the radio station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, we have a summary of what this witness is going to discuss. Can we go to it please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm aware of that. During proofing with this witness, I made some proofing notes and I informed the Prosecution about some few additional things that the witness might have knowledge about. I will go through this very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, please. Very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The instructions from the Chamber are such, and you are not a witness who could provide any significant information to us about the 4th Detachment and other things. I'm only asking you now: Do you know perhaps who was the commander of the detachment? Do you know whether Tadic and Zaric were members of it and what were their posts? So if you can just tell us that.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: I knew who the commander was. I knew that Zaric and Tadic were members of the 4th Detachment, but I didn't know what functions they were performing in the detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I would like to move to a different topic now. I am now talking about the end of 1991 and beginning of 1992, we are in the territory of the town and the municipality of Samac. Could you please tell us if you noticed whether there were any changes in the behaviour of the people in the security situation? Do you remember that period perhaps

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: Following the multiparty elections, the national parties won and formed the government. Provocators started cropping up in those parties who were abusing national symbols, thereby irritating members of other ethnic groups. Some songs began to appear of nationalistic content, which also irritated members of other ethnic groups. Rallies were being organised with inflammatory speeches, talking about how one ethnic group was being threatened by the other ethnic groups. This made the situation more complex and disrupted the interethnic relations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This was your assessment. There was a lot already said before the Trial Chamber about certain incidents which happened in the territory of the town and municipality of Bosanski Samac, and I do not wish to dwell on them with you too much, because a lot has already been said about them here. There was arson, explosions, and things of such nature. I'm interested in one such incident that you drew my attention to and about which you have some more detailed information, and this is the event relating to a certain gentleman called Simo Krunic. Could you please tell us what you know about that incident, what you heard about it, from whom?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: Simo Krunic is my neighbour. His house is about ten metres away from mine. I found out from him that on the 13th of April, in the afternoon, while he was at work - he was a member of the police force - he and his colleagues, Svetozar Mitrovic, were carrying out traffic checks not far from the bridge over the Sava River and were disarmed by, as he said, members of the Green Berets. On that occasion, their official pistols were confiscated, as well as their official radio station, Motorola. The confiscated items took the items and the attackers, let me call them that, went to Croatia [as interpreted]. The next day --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction. The attackers, let me call them that, took away the confiscated items and took them to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, on line [sic] 53, line 1, the confiscated items took the items and the attackers. It doesn't make much sense. Maybe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It's already been corrected, Mr. Lazarevic, by the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: -- immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Please continue. We had a mistake in the transcript. So what happened then?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: The next day, Dragan Lukac, as I said, who I think was the chief of the crime department in the public security station in Samac, went to Slavonski Brod and returned the confiscated items.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Just to clarify one thing: This Simo Krunic and this Mr. Mitrovic whom you mentioned, they were active police officers; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were active police officers out on their official duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And where did this happen? Did it happen in Bosanski Samac, in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. This happened on our side before the bridge, so it happened on the Bosnia-Herzegovina side.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now I would like to dwell on another topic. In the days before the 17th of April, 1992, where was your family? Where were your wife and your children?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: Three days before the outbreak of the conflict, on Monday, the children went to school. My son went to the seventh class and my daughter went to the first class. Me and my wife were at work. Sometime around 9.00, my son called me from home and said that they were all allowed to go home, they were all dismissed, and that there were no children at the school. I called my wife and told her what my child had told me. Both of us went home, and in view of the situation in the area, and the fact that Bosanski Brod was taken a while ago, that war was being waged in Croatia, and that weekend it was also noticed that many families belonging to all ethnic groups were taking their children out of Samac, to safer places.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And what did you do?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: Our relatives from Novi Sad suggested that we bring our children there as well, because following what was going on over the media, they were expecting that what happened in Bosanski Brod could also happen in Bosanski Samac. We decided to put our children into the car immediately. We told them to come to the border between Serbia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, to a place called Raca, and that is where I handed them over to them, together with my wife, and I returned home alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now I would like to go back briefly to what you were doing at that time. You said that practically from January 1st, 1988 you worked in the centre for reporting. Could you please first tell us: What is this reporting centre? What body is this? What are its duties? What are its tasks? Could you please explain to the Trial Chamber what this is so that they can have a more complete picture.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: The centre, the reporting centre, is an organisational unit that is part of the secretariat for National Defence. In the former Yugoslavia, each secretariat for National Defence had such reporting centres. The purpose of the centre is to collect certain data in the territory of the municipality where they were located, such as fires that break out, accidents, acts of sabotage, larger traffic accidents, floods, then to process this data and pass it on to the appropriate bodies. For that purpose, in the formation of the reporting centre, the citizens were informed, through different lectures and through the media, about the function of the reporting centre, in order to have access or to collect data more easily, the centre was connected with the local communities by telephone, and it also had radio connections with larger local communities. We called it the municipal radio link.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Some more clarifications regarding the centre itself. This was not a military reporting centre, was it?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: No, it wasn't a military centre, but it was a centre that was exclusively serving civilian needs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Did this centre have anything to do with the police or the state security or with any organs of that nature?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: No, it didn't have any connections with any of the bodies that you mentioned. As far as its range of activities --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I wanted to know.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: -- there was a telephone connection between the police station and us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: My question primarily refers to your range of activities. The police reporting centre was also talked about here before the Trial Chamber, so I wanted to just differentiate between the two of them. Could you please tell me now: You were explaining that there was a radio link between the municipal centre, where you worked in Samac, and other centres. Can you explain to me now: What were these other centres that there was a radio connection with?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, no. I said that first it was in the municipality, together with all the larger-scale local communes. There was a radio communication. We called it municipal radio link. The municipality of Samac belonged to the Doboj region, and it was on the level of the Doboj region that the regional centre for reporting was established. Its seat was in Doboj. Together with the regional centre, there were also municipal centres for reporting. Nine municipalities that made up the Doboj region, and these were Maglaj, Tesanj, Teslic, [Realtime transcript read in error "Maglag, Teslic"] Gracanica, Derventa, Bosanski Brod, Odzak, Samac, and Modrica. I think that I have listed them all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. Just one correction for the transcript. Actually, he may -- the witness also mentioned Tesanj. I will clarify with this, because there is one missing here. We have just seven municipalities and he was talking about eight municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was Tesanj also one of them?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, Tesanj was also one of them. Yes, Tesanj was also part of it. There were nine in total.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise. My mistake. Can you tell us now: How many employees were there at the centre while you worked there?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: If I may just clarify something in relation to these centres. We were all connected through radio link, and we called it the regional radio link. And above the regional centre, the reporting centre, was also the republican centre. Its seat was at the republic secretariat for National Defence, and that was located in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So if I understood you correctly, all of these nine municipalities that you listed, including Samac, they all had connection to each other, they were all mutually linked?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you now tell me: I asked you about the number of employees at the centre.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: When I came to the centre, which is in 1988, there were five of us in all. After the multiparty elections, the new authorities downsized the number of employees in the municipal administration, so in March 1992 there were three of us left.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to ask one other thing in relation to the centre. Can you tell us: Who was the duty officer in the centre for reporting in the night between the 16th and the 17th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: On that night, the duty officer was my colleague Ilija Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in the night between the 17th and the 18th of April, 1992, where were you [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: That night I was at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. There is some -- it's all right now. There is one mistake. My question was: The night between 16th and the 17th of April, where were you? Because that was my question, actually. Just that correction. This is what I asked the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, it will be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So you said that you were at home. Can you tell me: What happened in that night between the 16th and 17th of April? What did you see? What did you hear during that night?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: During that night, about 2.00 in the morning, I heard machine-gun bursts in the town. My house is about 800 metres, as the crow flies, from the centre of the town, and so it was possible to hear that machine-gun bursts very well. Sometime before dawn, I heard even more intense fire, so because I was supposed to go for my shift at 7.00 in the morning, at my place of work, about 6.00 I called him on the phone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. So the colleague who worked at the centre, you called him about 6.00 in the morning; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you pleas continue.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: When he answered the phone, he seemed quite scared, so I asked him what was happening in the town. He told me that there was shooting in the town but that he didn't know who was shooting, nor who were they shooting at. I told him that I would not be coming to work at 7.00 for my shift to replace him, for security reasons, until the situation calms down a little. I suggested to him that he should remain at the centre until the situation calms down. However, he told me that he had already been called several times by his wife, who is a mental patient, and that he should go home, because his wife was very scared to be at home with their daughter. I couldn't prevent him from doing that, so I told him to decide for himself what he should do further.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you go to work that day?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: No, I did not go to work that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us: What happened to that colleague of yours?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: My colleague Lukic, after we finished speaking, he went home, and on the way home was killed, which I found out two days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us: Did you hear how that happened? How was he killed?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, I did not hear how he was killed, but I know that he had a hearing problem, so I presume he didn't even hear anything as he was rushing to get home.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Just one other thing. Your colleague Ilija, what is his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: He was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me now: What happened further, on the 17th? What did you see? What happened to you?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: When the day broke, sometime after 7.00 in the morning, I went out into the yard to see what the situation was. In the street, I saw some of my neighbours, and I joined them. So we commented on the events that occurred in the night, but none of us had the right information regarding what was really happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: On that 17th of April, did anything else happen?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: After a short while, I went back into the house, and about 11.00 my neighbour, Milanko Misic, came and called me to come to Niko Ignjac's house. His house was located about a hundred metres away from my house, right next to the defence embankment of the right bank of the Bosna River.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you go to Niko Ignjac's house?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what was happening there?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: There I found several others of my neighbours, and a group of soldiers in uniforms, uniforms of the Yugoslav People's Army. There we were told that we should observe the right bank of the Bosna River, and we were given some tasks. For instance, together with my neighbour, Rada Radic, I was in his house, on the first floor, from where we observed the area across from the defence embankment, in the direction of the Bosna River.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So you were told to observe, to watch the embankment, and that's what you did; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me: How long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: In the evening, there was a roster of duties that was compiled, so there were duties in shifts, and I stayed there right until the 12th of May. Of course, during my time off I went home, because my home was nearby, and I would rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So you had a shift, during which you observed the bank, the river bank, after that, you had time off and then you went home. Is that what it was?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Now, can you tell me: During these first days after the 17th of April, 1992, did you go to the centre of the town?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: For the first ten days or so, I did not go into the town centre. I didn't go into the town. To start with, for security reasons, because there were rumours about snipers in town. After ten days or so, in the morning one day when I was free, when I had time off, that is, when I was not on my duty shift, I went into town, to the building of the secretariat for National Defence, to see who was there and to find out whether I was supposed to go to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me: On that occasion, who did you see? Who did you meet?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: At the building of the secretariat, I met only one colleague. His name is Milos Micic. We greeted each other. We talked a while, asked questions. I looked at the premises of the centre, where there was a lot of disorder. There were some sleeping bags there, and so I asked my colleague what had happened. His answer was that the premises of the centre, and some other premises of the secretariat, had been used by the members of the police for sleeping. After a while, I told him, since the secretary, Milos Bogdanovic, was not there, that he should tell him that I had come and that if I was supposed to work, they could find me in my locality, at the defence embankment, where I was on duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Now, can you tell me: Were you called? And if you were called, did you go to work again in the secretariat, at the reporting centre?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: On the 12th of May, I was informed by a messenger that I should come to the secretariat to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you go to the secretariat on the 12th of May?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, and there I was given a task by the secretary, Milos Bogdanovic, to activate the work of the inter-municipality, i.e., the regional radio link. Since the telephone lines were cut, and, as he told me, there were many parents whose children were in the JNA, so they wanted to get information through the centre about their fate.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me now: What did you find at the centre, and what did you do in order to implement the task given to you by Milos Bogdanovic?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: As I said before, the situation was disorderly, so first of all I implemented the physical cleaning of the premises, and then I obtained from the Master enterprise two batteries, since there was no electricity, because there was no electricity, so we needed them in order to operate the radio equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And did you manage to get the radio equipment to work?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. In two to three days, this was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me whether you started to maintain radio links with anybody, and if so, with whom, and how did that proceed?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: In order to test the radio links, I called my colleague at the Doboj regional centre and conducted an informal conversation with him in order to see whether the links were functioning, to test the reception, and generally to make it known that the Samac centre was operational, because at that point the other colleagues from neighbouring municipalities, which I mentioned earlier and which all were part of the Doboj region, were able to hear over their radios this conversation of ours and to find out that the reporting centre in Samac was operational.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Could you please wait for one moment now so that we could clarify one thing. So if you called Doboj from Samac and a link is established, do all of the other eight municipalities which have the same centres, with the same radio equipment, hear your conversation?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. The radio equipment is set up in such a way that we can all hear one another. But if I want to speak separately with a colleague, without disturbing the others, then I can agree with him to switch to a different channel where we can conduct our conversation. But all of this is heard by the other colleagues, so that if anyone was interested in our conversation, they can switch to that same channel and hear us again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can we summarise that in the following way: All nine municipalities were able to hear the conversations being held over the radio link?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have just a couple more questions about the radio link and maintenance of connections. Did the radio centre have a communication with the military centres?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: No, it didn't have a radio link with the military units.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And with the police?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: No, not with the police either, because these radio links were such that they were not compatible with their equipment and could not be used for communication in this sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me: In this period when you came, and in accordance with the order of Milos Bogdanovic, got the equipment to work on ACU [phoen] batteries, who else was working with you at the reporting centre?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: About a month, I was the only one working in the centre all day. Very often I stayed over during the night on duty. After about a month, upon my insistence, Secretary Milos engaged two retired police officers, Boro Savic and Milan Tutnjevic, and two other pensioners, Milan Jovanovic and Mico Antic, who took turns on duty during the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would now like to move to the topic of your contacts with the municipality of Odzak, with the people from Odzak. When did this take place for the first time, and how did it come about, this contact between the municipalities of Odzak and Samac?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: Sometime in late May - I don't remember the exact date - their secretary of the secretariat, Slavo Bago, requested, via the radio link, to talk to our secretary, Milos Bogdanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... for our break, usual break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, this is one very, very brief matter I want to raise with you, not related to this witness's evidence. If I could do that now. Given that it's almost 12.30. I simply wanted to ask you this: I understand that there's to be -- you request a response from the Prosecution on some further 92 bis statements and that you wish it to be -- the response to come tomorrow. All I ask is this: May I be permitted to reply orally or do you wish it to be a written motion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber was informed that the Prosecution has decided that they will put in a written reply by tomorrow on all the rest of the Rule 92 bis statements. MR. DI FAZIO: Very well. I'm sorry to have troubled you with it. The issue is settled. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We'll take our break for 20 minutes, resume at 12.50.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, before the break, we stopped at the point when a certain Slavko Bago wanted to speak with the secretary, Milos Bogdanovic. I assume, just to clarify one thing, that this Mr. Bago is from Odzak, is that right, he called from Odzak?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. He's the secretary of the secretariat for National Defence of Odzak, and he called from Odzak, from the reporting centre there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Could you please tell me: Did he talk to Mr. Bogdanovic on that occasion or not?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: Since Milos was not in the building, I told him that Milos wasn't there, so that this conversation did not take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Was there a conversation with Odzak at some point, during which Mr. Zaric was mentioned? Could you please tell us how this came about.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: A man was at the other side of the link. He said that he was a member of the Odzak Crisis Staff. Perhaps he introduced himself, told me his name, but I don't remember that now. He asked me if I knew Simo Zaric. I said that I did. He asked me if I could inform him to come tomorrow at 10.00, to be available at the radio link, and if he could, could he also bring a priest, a man called Puskaric.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, maybe just for the sake of safety, we should proceed in closed session for some -- sorry, not closed session; private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. I interrupted you so that we could cut short this part of the proceedings which was closed to the public. But now I would like to come back to the conversation of Simo Zaric and this man who called from Odzak and said that he had the authority of the Crisis Staff. So could you please tell us how that conversation continued, what you heard of it.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: When he said that he had the authority or the permission of the Crisis Staff to put Simo's family on the list, he told Simo that he had a pen and paper in front of him and that Simo could dictate to him the names of the family members that they would send to Samac. Simo then said that he didn't have enough paper to write down the names of all the relatives, family, and friends who were in Odzak. These words of Simo's made his collocutor from Odzak, the member of the Crisis Staff, angry, and he began to shout at Simo that he was not serious enough, that he was rude, and he also used some other insulting terms, and at the end said that in five or six days he would come to Samac, he would find Simo, and hang him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So the person from Samac -- from Odzak, from Odzak, was not satisfied with Simo's answer, and there was a verbal exchange between him and Mr. Zaric. Could you please tell us now what was the reaction of Mr. Zaric to that.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric broke off the connection at that point. He didn't wish to speak to him any longer, and he turned to those present and said: I do not wish to talk with this man any more and in this way. And he told me never to call him again, regardless of who asked for him to come over the radio link. After a short period, Simo left the centre. He went away.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this now. It's a detail relating to Mr. Zaric. Those two occasions when he came to the reporting centre, did he carry any lists with him other than what you heard and to the extent that you heard, was there any other discussions about people who would be placed on the list or removed from the list, anything in this context?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: When Simo came, he didn't have any lists, or he didn't have any notebooks to make notes in. While I was on the premises of the centre, I didn't hear anything relating to any exchange, nor was the term "exchange" mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Allow me to ask you one thing: When you were present at the centre premises, was there ever any talk about some captured pilots?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: No, there was never any talk about captured pilots.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You've told us now that there was this row, that Zaric disconnected the line and told you not to call him, regardless of who asked for him and for what reason. Could you please tell me: After this happened, and after Zaric left, did he ever come to the communication centre again? The reporting centre. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: They never asked for Mr. Zaric again, nor did he ever come to the reporting centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Sir, in the course of your work at the reporting centre at that time, did you keep any records or a log of calls and messages that you received, anything like that?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. After a certain amount of time, to be more precise, from the 22nd of June, due to more and more frequent conversations conducted between Odzak and Samac representatives, I began to keep notes of my own so that I would know at what time the conversations would be conducted, because the radio equipment ran on electricity which came from chargeable batteries, so it was necessary to conserve energy. That is why I kept a log, in order to know what would happen tomorrow and at what time the conversations were scheduled. And I would also then note down very briefly what happened in the course of a particular day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Before we move to the document itself, I would like to ask you one thing that we talked about during the preparation for this case. What do you know about the following: That at one point, in Bosanski Samac, a number of women of Croat ethnicity were gathered up and taken to a facility in Crkvina? Could you please tell us what you know about this event, and how did you find out about it?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: A friend of mine came to me - I don't remember the day that this happened - and asked me - he's actually married to a Croat woman - asked me if I could set up a connection or a line with Loznica, where she was staying, and inform her not to come home until he told her to do so because he had heard that women of Croat ethnicity were being collected, gathered together, and taken away somewhere. I wasn't able to help him, because the telephone lines weren't functioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So that is how you found out about that event. Do you know any other details about that event?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't know any other details about that, and I wasn't interested in finding out more.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can the witness be shown document D1543/ter. Yes for the record maybe it wasn't recorded that it was my question starting from "Can the witness be shown document." The way it is now in the transcript it looks like it is witness answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. It will be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And I believe that we have actually two documents, D104/3. One is in script, and the other was retyped. So I would like the witness to see the original, actually, the script in handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you've looked at this document. Could you please tell us what this is. Could you please put the document on the ELMO, next to you.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: This is a work book that was used, as it says here, on the 26th of November. This was in 1991. And we, the employees of the centre, noted down all the information that was passed on to the regional centre in the book. Later, when the conflicts began, there is a section in the notebook that I wrote, and there was some other handwritings, and these are by people who were at the centre when I wasn't there. Everything that I did from the 22nd of June is in this book.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Could you please turn to the part of the notebook where it begins: "From the 22nd of June," the period that you were recording the events. Could you please tell me: Is this your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is my handwriting, as of the 22nd. The handwriting above that is not my handwriting. This was written by somebody who happened to be in the centre, and they wrote down this information, and I think that this does not refer to the 22nd. This is a different date. As of the 22nd of June, 1992, this is my handwriting, and everything that is written down on the next page too is in my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... for my colleague. Yes, and may the record reflect that part of the text starting with 22nd of June, that the witness recognised his handwriting in this book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: In the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in this exhibit, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is not an exhibit; this is a document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: It's ID or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I believe that my colleague would like to give some explanation in respect to this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to say that we wanted to tender this document into evidence, and this document has an ID number, only because there were two different translations which the Prosecution brought up, and they wanted to compare that. But we did want to tender this document into evidence. This is a document that I named "The work book of the communications centre." There were two translations. There is a prior translation and then there was a later one, and the Prosecution wanted to have these two translations compared, and this is why the document was not tendered into evidence. I would just like to clarify one more thing. There is this notebook that the witness is looking at now. There is a transcript of the notebook, which was typed, which we did just in order to make the work of the interpreters easier, so they could read it more easily from the typing rather than to read the handwriting. So there is a transcript and there is the original notebook, the handwritten notebook.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The Prosecution, have you compared the translations?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Apparently there's some sort of typing that they had done and then a different translation was done by the Translation Unit, and they were supposed to compare it and tell us which one to use, and according to the case manager, we've never received any word from them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can you follow it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Which is valid. We've never received the typed one from Defence either, according to the case manager, that they've prepared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The typed one in Serbo-Croat?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No, we don't have that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am stating that we provided that to the Prosecution during the process of disclosure, and of course it was also given to them when we wished to tender it into evidence. I remember well providing the original document, the transcript in B/C/S, and the translation, and I will check back. I think the only problem is, allow me to remind you, when we wanted to reduce the amount of material from the notebook that needed to be translated, we decided, instead of translating only the part from the 22nd of June, we then decided to have the whole notebook translated, and this is this other part of the translation that came later. So first it was partially translated, and then the entire notebook was translated. Perhaps we could resolve this issue out of the courtroom, because I believe that this is a technical matter and that there won't be any other problems regarding the notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, rather than wasting the Court's time, we have a witness on the stand, I'll meet with counsel today and we'll get it all resolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I recall that the Defence were saying at one time that they only translated that which was relevant to their case. Yes. All right. The matter will be resolved by the parties afterwards. We can proceed with the witness. Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, this took up a little bit of our time. Could you please now look at this notebook. We're talking about the entries after the 22nd of June. Is the name of Mr. Zaric mentioned in any other place? Go ahead. Look at the notebook and tell us.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: I know for certain that Mr. Zaric's name is not mentioned anywhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would like to clarify a few more things about your work at the reporting centre. Could you please tell me: How long were you working at the reporting centre?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: From the 1st of September, 1992, those of us who worked at the secretariat for National Defence received new decisions on the schedule already in the defence ministry department of Samac, which means that the name of the body had changed, but the jobs remained the same. Under the new job descriptions and organisation, I was placed to carry out the duties of recruiting and mobilisation. After that, the work that I did at the reporting centre was something that I did as a secondary job, and I continued to carry out that work until the end of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The work that you did with the radio communications, was that much less than before?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: The amount of the work was reduced following the entry of the army of Republika Srpska to Bosanski Brod, because there were no more negotiations that were being conducted from the centre, because there was no radio communication from the other side with which negotiations could be established and could proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Now you were transferred to tasks relating to call-ups and mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the correction of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Sir, before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Before you proceed, the interpreters said they didn't catch the last words of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was actually overlapping. The witness actually corrected me because I said that he was working on mobilisation, and he said not mobilisation but recruitment and sending in to the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you can just repeat: What were the tasks that you were carrying out at the time?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC
utterances.text: As I said, with the new decision, I moved to a different job on recruiting and the sending of recruits to the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... 1345 is our usual time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We will rise and continue our proceedings tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
